newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S hopes for Asian open skies accords.
newsitem.headline: U.S hopes for Asian open skies accords.

text.p: The United States hopes that recent diplomatic contacts and talks with Asian officials will lead to a "critical mass" group of Asian countries ready to enter open skies agreements, a senior U.S. aviation official said on Tuesday.

Edward P.Oppler, deputy director at the U.S. Department of Transportation's Office of International Aviation, told an air cargo conference: "The U.S. will continue its bilateral efforts in Asia to obtain the most liberal aviation environments practically available to provide... the opportunity for better service and market-orientated rates."

Oppler added that an APEC (Asian-Pacific Economic Co-operation) working group had carried out some preliminary work on "more competitive air services with fair and equitable opportunity for all member economies".

Despite the opposition of some APEC countries, "there are some sectors of the aviation industry, such as the all-cargo sector, where opposition to liberalisation, whether bilateral or multilateral, might be less than in other areas such as passenger traffic," he noted.

Air cargo traffic between the U.S. and the Asia/Pacific countries between 1985 and 1995 increased to 1.8 million tons from some 700,000 tons, a rise of more than 150 percent, while U.S-Europe air cargo traffic rose 116 percent.
"In markets where liberal agreements were signed (in the past) air growth has been clearly facilitated and these markets compare dramatically with heavily restricted markets," Oppler said.
Thus between 1990 and 1995, freight tons carried in the liberalised Taiwan-U.S. market rose 280 percent, while in the U.S.-Japan market air cargo rose less than two percent.

Additionally air cargo liberalisation also requires the elimination of restrictions in areas related to cargo operations, if there is to be "a relationship responsive to the needs of participating carriers and the shipping public", he added.
He said these restrictions included customs clearance, ground handling, cargo warehousing and the provision of intermodal services, such as trucking.

Oppler said one example was the problem faced by Federal Express Corp in Thailand where despite the recent cargo agreement with the U.S., the Thai customs will not allow Fedex to carry express items on its own aircraft, but only via a courier on a normal passenger flight.

"We're trying to seek to resolve the issue. There is a Thai government working group on the issue, which includes representatives of express carriers and freight forwarders and hopefully it will be resolved," he said. -- Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
